title: Definition
body_md:
A set $S\subseteq V(G)$ is a dominating set of $G$ if $N[S]=V(G)$,
i.e.\ every vertex of $G$ lies in $S$ or is adjacent to a vertex of $S$.
A dominating set $S$ is minimal if no proper subset of $S$ is dominating;
equivalently, $S\setminus\{u\}$ is not dominating for every $u\in S$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $S\subseteq V(G)$ and $u\in S$. A vertex $w\in N[u]$ is called a
private neighbour of $u$ with respect to $S$ if $N[w]\cap S=\{u\}$,
i.e.\ $u$ is the only vertex of $S$ that dominates $w$.
(Note that $w=u$ is allowed.)
head: environment

label: lem:private
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S$ be a dominating set of $G$. We prove both directions.\\
 Assume $S$ is minimal, and let $u \in S$ be arbitrary. By minimality, $S \setminus \{u\}$ is not dominating. Hence there exists $w \in V(G)$ such that
$
N[w] \cap (S \setminus \{u\}) = \varnothing.
$
Since $S$ is dominating, $N[w] \cap S \neq \varnothing$. Because $S = (S \setminus \{u\}) \cup \{u\}$, we obtain
$
N[w] \cap S = \{u\}.
$\\
In particular $u \in N[w]$, and by symmetry of the closed neighbourhood, $w \in N[u]$. Thus $w$ is a private neighbour of $u$ with respect to $S$. Since $u \in S$ was arbitrary, every vertex of $S$ has a private neighbour.\\
Now, assume every $u \in S$ has a private neighbour. Fix $u \in S$ and let $w \in N[u]$ be a private neighbour of $u$, i.e.
$
N[w] \cap S = \{u\}.
$
Then
$
N[w] \cap (S \setminus \{u\}) = \varnothing,
$
and $w \notin S \setminus \{u\}$ (otherwise $w \in N[w] \cap (S \setminus \{u\})$, a contradiction). Hence $w$ is not dominated by $S \setminus \{u\}$, so $S \setminus \{u\}$ is not dominating. Since $u \in S$ was arbitrary, no proper subset of $S$ obtained by deleting a single vertex is dominating; equivalently, $S$ is minimal.
head: environment

label: lem:delta1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v \in V(G)$ be arbitrary.\\
Step 1. Extend the independent set $\{v\}$ to a maximal
independent set $I$ (possible by a greedy argument). Then $v \in I$.\\
Step 2. We claim that $I$ is a dominating set. Suppose
otherwise: there exists $x \in V(G)$ such that $x \notin I$ and $x$ is
adjacent to no vertex of $I$. Then $I \cup \{x\}$ is also an independent
set, contradicting the maximality of $I$. Hence $I$ is dominating.\\
Step 3. We claim that $I$ is a \emph{minimal}
dominating set. Let $u \in I$. Since $I$ is independent, no vertex of
$I \setminus \{u\}$ is equal or adjacent to $u$; in particular,
$u \notin I \setminus \{u\}$ and $N[u] \cap (I \setminus \{u\}) = \varnothing$.
Hence $I \setminus \{u\}$ does not dominate $u$. Since $u \in I$ was
arbitrary, $I$ is minimal.\\
By Steps 1--3, $I$ is a minimal dominating
set containing $v$. Since $v \in V(G)$ was arbitrary, every vertex of
$G$ lies in a minimal dominating set, which implies
\[
\delta_d = \min_{v \in V(G)} d_d(v) \ge 1. \qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: thm:elementary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:elementary}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
\frac{m}{2\Delta_d^2} \le DRMS(G) \le \frac{m}{2\delta_d^2}.
\]
Equality holds in either bound if and only if $G$ is
$k$-domination-regular for some $k \ge 1$; in that case,
$
DRMS(G) = \frac{m}{2k^2}.
$
head: environment

label: eq:basic-ineq
title: Proof
body_md:
For every edge $uv \in E(G)$, since $\delta_d \le d_d(x) \le \Delta_d$ for all $x$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:basic-ineq}
2\delta_d^2 \le d_d^2(u) + d_d^2(v) \le 2\Delta_d^2.
\end{equation}
\emph{Lower bound.} From the right side of \eqref{eq:basic-ineq},
$d_d^2(u)+d_d^2(v) \le 2\Delta_d^2$ for every edge, so
$\frac{1}{d_d^2(u)+d_d^2(v)} \ge \frac{1}{2\Delta_d^2}$.
Summing over the $m$ edges gives $DRMS(G) \ge \frac{m}{2\Delta_d^2}$.\\
\emph{Upper bound.} Similarly, from the left side of \eqref{eq:basic-ineq},
$\frac{1}{d_d^2(u)+d_d^2(v)} \le \frac{1}{2\delta_d^2}$, and summing gives
$DRMS(G) \le \frac{m}{2\delta_d^2}$.\\
\emph{Equality.} Each summand in $DRMS(G) - \frac{m}{2\Delta_d^2}$ is nonnegative,
so the sum vanishes if and only if every summand vanishes, i.e.\ if and only if
$d_d^2(u)+d_d^2(v) = 2\Delta_d^2$ for every edge $uv$. Since
$d_d^2(x) \le \Delta_d^2$, this forces $d_d(u)=d_d(v)=\Delta_d$ on every edge,
hence $d_d \equiv \Delta_d$ by connectedness. The upper-bound case is symmetric:
equality holds if and only if $d_d \equiv \delta_d$. In either case $d_d\equiv k$, and
$
DRMS(G) = \sum_{uv \in E} \frac{1}{2k^2} = \frac{m}{2k^2}. \qedhere
$
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
If $G$ is $k$-domination-regular with $m$ edges, then
\[
DRMS(G)=\frac{m}{2k^2}.
\]
head: environment

label: thm:max
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:max}
For every connected graph $G$ of order $n\ge2$,
\[
DRMS(G)\ \le\ \frac m2\ \le\ \frac{n(n-1)}4 .
\]
Equality holds in the first inequality if and only if $d_d\equiv1$, and in the
second if and only if $G=K_n$. In particular,
$\max_G DRMS(G)=n(n-1)/4$ over connected graphs of order $n$, and it is
attained only by $K_n$. Moreover, every tree $T$ of order $n$ satisfies
$DRMS(T)\le (n-1)/2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:delta1} we have $d_d\ge1$, so $x_e=a_e^{2}+b_e^{2}\ge2$ and
$1/x_e\le1/2$ for every edge $e$, with equality if and only if
$a_e=b_e=1$. Summing over $E(G)$ gives $DRMS(G)\le m/2$, with equality if and
only if $a_e=b_e=1$ for every edge $e$. Since $G$ is connected and $n\ge2$,
every vertex lies on an edge, so this holds if and only if $d_d\equiv1$ (and
if $d_d\equiv1$, then $x_e=2$ for all $e$, so equality indeed holds). Next,
$m\le n(n-1)/2$ with equality if and only if $G=K_n$, which gives the second
inequality and its equality case. Every vertex of $K_n$ lies in exactly one
minimal dominating set (the singletons), so $d_d\equiv1$ on $K_n$ and
$DRMS(K_n)=\frac12\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}2=\frac{n(n-1)}4$. Hence the maximum is
$n(n-1)/4$. If $DRMS(G)=n(n-1)/4$, then both inequalities of the chain are
equalities; in particular $m=n(n-1)/2$, so $G=K_n$. Finally, a tree has
$m=n-1$ edges, so $DRMS(T)\le m/2=(n-1)/2$.
head: environment

label: thm:pmean
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:pmean}
For every connected graph \(G\) and every \(p \in [-1, 1]\),
\[
DRMS(G) \ge \frac{m}{M_p(x)}.
\]
For \(p > -1\), equality holds if and only if \(x_e\) is constant over
\(E(G)\); for \(p = -1\), equality always holds.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
\[
DRMS(G) = \sum_{e \in E(G)} x_e^{-1}
= \left( \frac{1}{m} \sum_{e \in E(G)} x_e^{-1} \right)^{-1} \cdot \frac{1}{m} \cdot m
= \frac{m}{M_{-1}(x)},
\]
the claimed inequality \(DRMS(G) \ge m/M_p(x)\) is equivalent to
\[
M_{-1}(x) \le M_p(x).
\]
This is the monotonicity of the power mean in its order: for \(q \le p\),
\(M_q(x) \le M_p(x)\). Taking \(q = -1\) and \(p \ge -1\) gives the claim.\\
\emph{Equality.} The function \(p \mapsto M_p(x)\) is strictly increasing
unless all \(x_e\) coincide; hence for \(p > -1\), equality \(M_{-1}(x) = M_p(x)\)
holds if and only if \(x_e\) is constant over \(E(G)\). For \(p = -1\), both
sides equal \(DRMS(G)\) trivially, so equality always holds.

label: cor:pmean-special
title: Corollary

label: thm:cauchy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cauchy}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
DRMS(G) \ge \frac{m^2}{DF^*(G)}.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $x_e$ is constant over all edges $e \in E(G)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Cauchy--Schwarz to the sequences
\[
p_e := \sqrt{x_e}, \qquad q_e := \frac{1}{\sqrt{x_e}} \qquad (e \in E(G)).
\]
Then $p_e q_e = 1$, $p_e^2 = x_e$, and $q_e^2 = 1/x_e$, so
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{e \in E} 1\Bigr)^2
\le \Bigl(\sum_{e \in E} x_e\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{e \in E} \frac{1}{x_e}\Bigr)
= DF^*(G) \cdot DRMS(G).
\]
Since $x_e \ge 2\delta_d^2 \ge 2 > 0$ for every edge (by Lemma \ref{lem:delta1}), we have
$DF^*(G) > 0$, so dividing by $DF^*(G)$ yields
\[
DRMS(G) \ge \frac{m^2}{DF^*(G)}.
\]
Equality in Cauchy--Schwarz holds if and only if the sequences $p_e$ and
$q_e$ are proportional, which means there exists a constant $\lambda$ such
that $p_e = \lambda\, q_e$ for every $e \in E(G)$. Substituting
$p_e = \sqrt{x_e}$ and $q_e = 1/\sqrt{x_e}$ gives
$
\sqrt{x_e} = \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{x_e}},
$
and hence $x_e = \lambda$ for every edge. Therefore equality holds if and only
if $x_e$ is constant over all edges $e \in E(G)$.
head: environment

label: thm:interval
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:interval}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
DRMS(G) \le \frac{2m(\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2) - DF^*(G)}{4\delta_d^2 \Delta_d^2}.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $x_e \in \{2\delta_d^2, 2\Delta_d^2\}$ for every
edge $e \in E(G)$.
head: environment

label: eq:interval-aux
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $x_- = 2\delta_d^2$ and $x_+ = 2\Delta_d^2$. For every $x \in [x_-, x_+]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:interval-aux}
\frac{1}{x} \le \frac{x_- + x_+ - x}{x_-x_+}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, multiplying both sides by $x_-x_+x > 0$ gives
$x_-x_+ \le (x_- + x_+ - x)x$, which rearranges to $(x - x_-)(x_+ - x) \ge 0$;
the latter holds because $x \in [x_-, x_+]$.\\
By the basic inequality $2\delta_d^2 \le x_e \le 2\Delta_d^2$, every edge
satisfies $x_e \in [x_-, x_+]$. Applying \eqref{eq:interval-aux} to $x = x_e$
and summing over all $e \in E(G)$,
\[
DRMS(G) = \sum_{e \in E} \frac{1}{x_e}
\le \sum_{e \in E} \frac{x_- + x_+ - x_e}{x_-x_+}
= \frac{1}{x_-x_+}\Bigl[(x_- + x_+)m - \sum_{e \in E} x_e\Bigr].
\]
Substituting $x_- = 2\delta_d^2$, $x_+ = 2\Delta_d^2$, $x_-x_+ = 4\delta_d^2 \Delta_d^2$,
and $\sum_{e \in E} x_e = DF^*(G)$ yields the claimed inequality.\\
\emph{Equality condition.} Since the sum
\[
\frac{1}{x_-x_+}\Bigl[(x_- + x_+)m - DF^*(G)\Bigr] - DRMS(G)
= \sum_{e \in E}\Bigl[\frac{x_- + x_+ - x_e}{x_-x_+} - \frac{1}{x_e}\Bigr]
\]
is a sum of nonnegative terms by \eqref{eq:interval-aux}, it vanishes if and
only if every term vanishes, that is, if and only if
\[
\frac{x_- + x_+ - x_e}{x_-x_+} = \frac{1}{x_e} \quad \text{for every } e \in E(G).
\]
By the factorization $(x_e - x_-)(x_+ - x_e) = 0$ established above, this is
equivalent to $x_e = x_-$ or $x_e = x_+$ for every edge. In other words,
equality holds if and only if
\[
x_e \in \{2\delta_d^2,\, 2\Delta_d^2\} \quad \text{for every } e \in E(G).
\qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: thm:kantorovich
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:kantorovich}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
DRMS(G) \le \frac{m^2}{DF^*(G)}
\left(\frac{\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2}{2\delta_d \Delta_d}\right)^2.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $x_e \in \{2\delta_d^2, 2\Delta_d^2\}$ for every
edge $e \in E(G)$.
head: environment

label: eq:kantorovich
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $x_- = 2\delta_d^2$ and $x_+ = 2\Delta_d^2$. By the basic inequality,
$x_e \in [x_-, x_+]$ for every edge $e \in E(G)$. The Kantorovich inequality
for a sequence $(x_e)_{e \in E(G)}$ in $[x_-, x_+]$ states that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kantorovich}
\Bigl(\sum_{e \in E} x_e\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{e \in E} \frac{1}{x_e}\Bigr)
\le m^2 \cdot \frac{(x_- + x_+)^2}{4x_-x_+}.
\end{equation}
Substituting $\sum_{e \in E} x_e = DF^*(G)$, $\sum_{e \in E} 1/x_e = DRMS(G)$,
$x_- + x_+ = 2(\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2)$, and $x_-x_+ = 4\delta_d^2 \Delta_d^2$ gives
\[
DF^*(G) \cdot DRMS(G) \le m^2 \cdot \frac{(\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2)^2}{4\delta_d^2 \Delta_d^2}.
\]
Dividing both sides by $DF^*(G) > 0$ and rewriting the constant factor yields
\[
DRMS(G) \le \frac{m^2}{DF^*(G)}
\left(\frac{\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2}{2\delta_d \Delta_d}\right)^2.
\]
\emph{Equality condition.} Equality in \eqref{eq:kantorovich} holds if and only
if each $x_e$ takes only the values $x_-$ and $x_+$, that is, if and only if
$x_e \in \{2\delta_d^2, 2\Delta_d^2\}$ for every edge $e \in E(G)$.
\qedhere
head: environment

label: thm:dm2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:dm2}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
DRMS(G)\ \ge\ \frac{\delta_d\Delta_d}{\delta_d^{2}+\Delta_d^{2}}\cdot\frac{m^{2}}{DM_2(G)}.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $\{d_d(u),d_d(v)\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$
for every edge $uv\in E(G)$ when $\delta_d<\Delta_d$, and for all edges
(i.e. $G$ is domination-regular) when $\delta_d=\Delta_d$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\gamma_d=\dfrac{\delta_d\Delta_d}{\delta_d^{2}+\Delta_d^{2}}$. For an edge $e=uv$
recall $a_e=d_d(u)$ and $b_e=d_d(v)$; by symmetry we may assume $a_e\ge b_e$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:delta1}, $\delta_d\ge 1$, so all quantities below are well defined.

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Step 1 (edgewise inequality).}
Let $r=a_e/b_e$. Since $\delta_d\le b_e\le a_e\le\Delta_d$, we have
$1\le r\le \Delta_d/\delta_d$, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dm2-t}
r=\frac{\Delta_d}{\delta_d}
\quad\text{if and only if}\quad
a_e=\Delta_d\ \text{and}\ b_e=\delta_d .
\end{equation}
(Indeed $a_e/b_e\le \Delta_d/\delta_d$ because $a_e\le\Delta_d$ and $b_e\ge\delta_d$,
and equality forces both of these to be equalities.)
The function $f(r)=r+1/r$ satisfies $f'(r)=1-1/r^{2}\ge 0$ on $[1,\infty)$ and is
strictly increasing there. Hence
\[
\frac{a_e^{2}+b_e^{2}}{a_e b_e}=\frac{a_e}{b_e}+\frac{b_e}{a_e}=f(r)
\le f\!\left(\frac{\Delta_d}{\delta_d}\right)
=\frac{\Delta_d}{\delta_d}+\frac{\delta_d}{\Delta_d}
=\frac{\Delta_d^{2}+\delta_d^{2}}{\delta_d\Delta_d},
\]
and, by strict monotonicity and \eqref{eq:dm2-t}, equality holds if and only if
$\{a_e,b_e\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$ when $\delta_d<\Delta_d$ (when
$\delta_d=\Delta_d$ both sides equal $2$ for every edge). Taking reciprocals,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dm2-edgewise}
\frac{1}{x_e}=\frac{1}{a_e^{2}+b_e^{2}}\ \ge\ \gamma_d\,\frac{1}{a_e b_e}\qquad(e\in E(G)),
\end{equation}
with equality if and only if $\{a_e,b_e\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$ (or $\delta_d=\Delta_d$).

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Step 2 (summation).}
Summing \eqref{eq:dm2-edgewise} over all edges gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dm2-sum}
DRMS(G)\ \ge\ \gamma_d\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{a_e b_e}.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Step 3 (Cauchy--Schwarz).}
Applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to the sequences
$\sqrt{a_e b_e}$ and $1/\sqrt{a_e b_e}$ $(e\in E(G))$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dm2-cs}
m^{2}=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}1\Bigr)^{2}
\le \Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e b_e\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{a_e b_e}\Bigr)
= DM_2(G)\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{a_e b_e}.
\end{equation}
Since $DM_2(G)>0$, this gives $\sum_{e}1/(a_e b_e)\ge m^{2}/DM_2(G)$.
Combining with \eqref{eq:dm2-sum},
\[
DRMS(G)\ \ge\ \gamma_d\,\frac{m^{2}}{DM_2(G)},
\]
which is the claimed inequality.

\medskip
\noindent\textit{Equality.}
Write
\[
DRMS(G)-\gamma_d\frac{m^{2}}{DM_2(G)}
=\sum_{e}\Bigl(\frac1{x_e}-\frac{\gamma_d}{a_e b_e}\Bigr)
+\;\gamma_d\Bigl(\sum_{e}\frac1{a_e b_e}-\frac{m^{2}}{DM_2(G)}\Bigr) .
\]
By \eqref{eq:dm2-edgewise} the first sum is nonnegative, and by
\eqref{eq:dm2-cs} the second sum is nonnegative. Hence the right-hand side is
nonnegative, with equality if and only if both sums vanish.\\
If equality holds, the first bracket is a sum of nonnegative
terms and vanishes, so equality holds in \eqref{eq:dm2-edgewise} for every edge; by Step~1 every
edge $e$ satisfies $\{a_e,b_e\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$ (or $\delta_d=\Delta_d$).\\
Suppose every edge satisfies $\{a_e,b_e\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$
(or $\delta_d=\Delta_d$). Then equality holds in \eqref{eq:dm2-edgewise} for each $e$, so the first
bracket is $0$. Moreover $a_e b_e=\delta_d\Delta_d$ is constant over $E(G)$, so
the sequences $\sqrt{a_e b_e}$ and $1/\sqrt{a_e b_e}$ are proportional and equality
holds in \eqref{eq:dm2-cs}; the second bracket is $0$ as well.

title: Remark
body_md:
If $\delta_d<\Delta_d$, a connected graph in which every edge joins a vertex of
degree $\delta_d$ to one of degree $\Delta_d$ is bipartite, with the two classes
given by the two values of $d_d$. For $K_{2,3}$ we have $d_d\in\{4,3\}$,
$m=6$, $DM_2(K_{2,3})=72$, and
$\frac{12}{25}\cdot\frac{36}{72}=0.24=DRMS(K_{2,3})$, so the bound is attained
although $K_{2,3}$ is not domination-regular.

label: thm:db1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:db1}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
DRMS(G)\ge
\frac{m^2}{2\,\Delta_d\,DB_1(G)}.
\]
Moreover, equality holds if and only if $G$ is domination-regular.
head: environment

label: eq:db1-edge
title: Proof
body_md:
For an edge $e=uv$ recall $a_e=d_d(u)$, $b_e=d_d(v)$, $x_e=a_e^{2}+b_e^{2}$ and
$\sigma_e=a_e+b_e$. By Lemma \ref{lem:delta1} we have $\delta_d\ge 1$, so $a_e,b_e,\sigma_e,x_e>0$
and all quotients below are well defined. By Definition \ref{2.4},
$\sum_{e\in E(G)}\sigma_e=2\,DB_1(G)$.\\
Since $a_e,b_e\le\Delta_d$ for every edge $e$,
\[
\Delta_d\,\sigma_e-x_e=a_e(\Delta_d-a_e)+b_e(\Delta_d-b_e)\ \ge\ 0,
\]
hence $x_e\le\Delta_d\,\sigma_e$, that is,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:db1-edge}
\frac{1}{x_e}\ \ge\ \frac{1}{\Delta_d\,\sigma_e}\qquad(e\in E(G)).
\end{equation}
Both summands above are nonnegative and $a_e,b_e>0$, so equality holds in
\eqref{eq:db1-edge} if and only if $a_e=b_e=\Delta_d$. Summing
\eqref{eq:db1-edge} over all edges gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:db1-sum}
DRMS(G)=\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{x_e}\ \ge\ \frac{1}{\Delta_d}\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{\sigma_e}.
\end{equation}
Applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to the sequences $\sqrt{\sigma_e}$ and
$1/\sqrt{\sigma_e}$ $(e\in E(G))$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:db1-cs}
m^{2}=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}1\Bigr)^{2}
\le\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}\sigma_e\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{\sigma_e}\Bigr)
=2\,DB_1(G)\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac{1}{\sigma_e}.
\end{equation}
Since $DB_1(G)>0$, this gives $\sum_{e}1/\sigma_e\ge m^{2}/\bigl(2\,DB_1(G)\bigr)$,
and combining with \eqref{eq:db1-sum} yields
\[
DRMS(G)\ \ge\ \frac{m^{2}}{2\,\Delta_d\,DB_1(G)} .
\]
For the equality case, write
\[
DRMS(G)-\frac{m^{2}}{2\Delta_d DB_1(G)}
=\sum_{e\in E(G)}\Bigl(\frac1{x_e}-\frac1{\Delta_d\sigma_e}\Bigr)
+\frac1{\Delta_d}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}\frac1{\sigma_e}-\frac{m^{2}}{2DB_1(G)}\Bigr).
\]
The first sum is nonnegative by \eqref{eq:db1-edge} and the bracket is nonnegative
by \eqref{eq:db1-cs}; hence equality holds in the theorem if and only if both
vanish. If equality holds, then every term of the first sum vanishes, so equality
holds in \eqref{eq:db1-edge} for every edge, i.e.\ $a_e=b_e=\Delta_d$ for every
$e=uv\in E(G)$. As $G$ is connected, every vertex lies on an edge, so
$d_d\equiv\Delta_d$ and $G$ is domination-regular. Conversely, if $d_d\equiv k$
for some $k\ge1$, then $\Delta_d=k$, $\sigma_e=2k$ and $x_e=2k^{2}$ for every
edge, so $DB_1(G)=mk$ and
\[
\frac{m^{2}}{2\Delta_d DB_1(G)}=\frac{m^{2}}{2k\cdot mk}=\frac{m}{2k^{2}}=DRMS(G)
\]
head: environment

label: cor:db1-sharp
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:db1-sharp}
If $G$ is $k$-domination-regular, then $DB_1(G)=mk$ and
\[
DRMS(G)=\frac{m}{2k^2}
=
\frac{m^2}{2\,\Delta_d\,DB_1(G)}.
\]
Hence the bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:db1} is attained.
head: environment

label: lem:kappa
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:kappa}
For every edge $e$,
\[
\kappa_d\ \le\ \frac{\sigma_e}{\sqrt{x_e}}\ \le\ \sqrt2 .
\]
The right equality holds if and only if $a_e=b_e$; the left one holds if and only if
$\{a_e,b_e\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$ or $\delta_d=\Delta_d$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\sigma_e^{2}=x_e+2a_eb_e$ and $a_eb_e/x_e=\bigl(a_e/b_e+b_e/a_e\bigr)^{-1}$,
\[
\frac{\sigma_e^{2}}{x_e}=1+\frac{2}{a_e/b_e+b_e/a_e}.
\]
Put $r=\max\{a_e,b_e\}/\min\{a_e,b_e\}$, so that $a_e/b_e+b_e/a_e=f(r)$ with
$f(r)=r+1/r$ and $1\le r\le\Delta_d/\delta_d$. The function $f$ is strictly increasing on $[1,\infty)$, hence
\[
2=f(1)\ \le\ a_e/b_e+b_e/a_e\ \le\ f\!\left(\tfrac{\Delta_d}{\delta_d}\right)
=\frac{\Delta_d^{2}+\delta_d^{2}}{\delta_d\Delta_d}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\kappa_d^{2}=1+\frac{2\delta_d\Delta_d}{\delta_d^{2}+\Delta_d^{2}}\ \le\
\frac{\sigma_e^{2}}{x_e}\ \le\ 2 ,
\]
and taking square roots gives the claim. By strict monotonicity of $f$, the
upper bound is attained if and only if $r=1$, i.e.\ $a_e=b_e$, and the lower bound is
attained if and only if $r=\Delta_d/\delta_d$, i.e.\ $\{a_e,b_e\}=\{\delta_d,\Delta_d\}$
when $\delta_d<\Delta_d$; if $\delta_d=\Delta_d$ then $a_e=b_e$, both
bounds equal $\sqrt2$ and the lower equality holds trivially.
head: environment

label: thm:so
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:so}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
DRMS(G)\ \ge\ \frac{m^{3}}{SO_d(G)^{2}}.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $x_e$ is constant over $E(G)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lem:delta1} we have $\delta_d\ge1$, so $x_e>0$ for every edge $e$. Apply
H\"older's inequality with the conjugate exponents $3$ and $3/2$ to the
positive sequences $x_e^{-1/3}$ and $x_e^{1/3}$ $(e\in E(G))$, we obtain
\[
m=\sum_{e\in E(G)}x_e^{-1/3}x_e^{1/3}
\le\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}x_e^{-1}\Bigr)^{1/3}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E(G)}x_e^{1/2}\Bigr)^{2/3}
=DRMS(G)^{1/3}\,SO_d(G)^{2/3}.
\]
Cubing gives $m^{3}\le DRMS(G)\,SO_d(G)^{2}$, and since $SO_d(G)>0$ the
claimed inequality follows. Equality in H\"older's inequality holds if and only if the
sequences $\bigl(x_e^{-1/3}\bigr)^{3}=x_e^{-1}$ and
$\bigl(x_e^{1/3}\bigr)^{3/2}=x_e^{1/2}$ are proportional, that is,
$x_e^{-1}=\lambda\,x_e^{1/2}$ for some constant $\lambda>0$ and all $e$. This
means $x_e^{3/2}=1/\lambda$, so $x_e$ is constant over $E(G)$. Conversely, if
$x_e\equiv x$, then $DRMS(G)=m/x$ and $SO_d(G)=m\sqrt{x}$, hence
$m^{3}/SO_d(G)^{2}=m/x=DRMS(G)$.
head: environment

label: thm:mdso
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mdso}
For every connected graph $G$,
\[
\frac{{}^{m}SO_d(G)^{2}}{m}\ \le\ DRMS(G)\ \le\
\frac{\delta_d+\Delta_d}{\sqrt2\,\delta_d\Delta_d}\,{}^{m}SO_d(G)-\frac{m}{2\delta_d\Delta_d}.
\]
Equality holds on the left if and only if $x_e$ is constant over $E(G)$, and
on the right if and only if $G$ is domination-regular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lem:delta1}, $x_e>0$ for every edge $e$, so $y_e:=x_e^{-1/2}$ is well defined,
and $DRMS(G)=\sum_{e}y_e^{2}$, ${}^{m}SO_d(G)=\sum_{e}y_e$. Put
\[
y_-=\frac{1}{\sqrt2\,\Delta_d},\qquad y_+=\frac{1}{\sqrt2\,\delta_d}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:basic-ineq}, $2\delta_d^{2}\le x_e\le2\Delta_d^{2}$, hence $y_-\le y_e\le y_+$ for
every edge $e$.\\
By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
$\bigl(\sum_e y_e\bigr)^{2}\le m\sum_e y_e^{2}$, which is the left inequality;
equality holds if and only if $y_e$ is constant, that is, if and only if $x_e$ is constant. For the
right inequality, $(y_e-y_-)(y_+-y_e)\ge0$ gives
$y_e^{2}\le(y_-+y_+)\,y_e-y_-y_+$ for every edge. Summing over $E(G)$,
\[
DRMS(G)\le(y_-+y_+)\,{}^{m}SO_d(G)-m\,y_-y_+,
\]
and inserting $y_-+y_+=\dfrac{\delta_d+\Delta_d}{\sqrt2\,\delta_d\Delta_d}$ and
$y_-y_+=\dfrac{1}{2\delta_d\Delta_d}$ gives the claim. The difference between
the two sides equals $\sum_{e}(y_e-y_-)(y_+-y_e)$, a sum of nonnegative terms,
so equality holds if and only if $y_e\in\{y_-,y_+\}$ for every edge, that is,
$x_e\in\{2\Delta_d^{2},2\delta_d^{2}\}$. Since $\delta_d\le a_e,b_e\le\Delta_d$,
$x_e=2\delta_d^{2}$ forces $a_e=b_e=\delta_d$ and $x_e=2\Delta_d^{2}$ forces
$a_e=b_e=\Delta_d$. Thus equality implies that both endpoints of every edge
have the same domination degree, so $d_d$ is constant along every path; as $G$
is connected, $d_d$ is constant on $V(G)$ and $G$ is domination-regular.
Conversely, if $d_d\equiv k$, then $\delta_d=\Delta_d=k$ and
$y_e=y_-=y_+=\dfrac1{\sqrt2\,k}$ for every edge, so each term
$(y_e-y_-)(y_+-y_e)$ vanishes and equality holds; both sides equal
$m/(2k^{2})$.
head: environment

label: thm:deso
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:deso}
Let \(G\) be a connected graph. Then
\[
\frac{\kappa_d \, m^2}{DESO(G)} \le DRMS(G) \le \frac{\sqrt{2} \, c_d \, m^2}{DESO(G)},
\]
where, $
\kappa_d = \frac{\delta_d + \Delta_d}{\sqrt{\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2}}, c_d = \left(\frac{\delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2}{2\delta_d \Delta_d}\right)^2.
$ \\
Equality on the left holds if and only if every edge joins a vertex of
domination degree \(\delta_d\) to one of domination degree \(\Delta_d\)
(or \(\delta_d = \Delta_d\)); equality on the right holds if and only if \(G\)
is domination-regular.
head: environment

label: eq:deso-i
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}, \(\kappa_d \sqrt{x_e} \le \sigma_e \le \sqrt{2} \sqrt{x_e}\)
for every edge \(e \in E(G)\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{x_e}\) and summing over
all edges gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deso-i}
\kappa_d \, DF^*(G) \le DESO(G) \le \sqrt{2} \, DF^*(G).
\end{equation}
By Theorems~\ref{thm:cauchy} and~\ref{thm:kantorovich},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deso-ii}
m^2 \le DF^*(G) \cdot DRMS(G) \le c_d \, m^2.
\end{equation}\\
\emph{Lower bound.} Multiplying the left inequalities of
\eqref{eq:deso-i} and \eqref{eq:deso-ii},
\[
DESO(G) \cdot DRMS(G) \ge \kappa_d \, DF^*(G) \cdot DRMS(G) \ge \kappa_d \, m^2.
\]
Dividing by \(DESO(G) > 0\) gives \(DRMS(G) \ge \kappa_d m^2 / DESO(G)\).\\
\emph{Upper bound.} Multiplying the right inequalities,
\[
DESO(G) \cdot DRMS(G) \le \sqrt{2} \, DF^*(G) \cdot DRMS(G) \le \sqrt{2} \, c_d \, m^2.
\]
Dividing by \(DESO(G) > 0\) gives
\(DRMS(G) \le \sqrt{2} \, c_d m^2 / DESO(G)\).\\
\emph{Equality, left.} It requires equality in both \eqref{eq:deso-i} (left)
and \eqref{eq:deso-ii} (left). By the equality condition of
Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}, the former forces \(\sigma_e/\sqrt{x_e} = \kappa_d\) on
every edge, that is, \(\{a_e, b_e\} = \{\delta_d, \Delta_d\}\) or
\(\delta_d = \Delta_d\). Conversely, if every edge satisfies
\(\{a_e, b_e\} = \{\delta_d, \Delta_d\}\), then
\[
x_e = a_e^2 + b_e^2 = \delta_d^2 + \Delta_d^2
\]
is constant over \(E(G)\), so equality holds in the Cauchy--Schwarz bound
\eqref{eq:deso-ii} (left). Hence equality on the left holds under the stated
condition.\\
\emph{Equality, right.} It requires equality in both \eqref{eq:deso-i} (right)
and \eqref{eq:deso-ii} (right). By the equality condition of
Lemma~\ref{lem:kappa}, the former forces \(\sigma_e = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{x_e}\), that
is, \(a_e = b_e\) on every edge. Since \(G\) is connected, this implies
\(d_d \equiv k\) on \(V(G)\), that is, \(G\) is domination-regular.
Conversely, if \(d_d \equiv k\), then \(\delta_d = \Delta_d = k\), so
\[
c_d = \left(\frac{k^2 + k^2}{2k^2}\right)^2 = 1,
\]
and \(a_e = b_e\) for every edge, so all inequalities become equalities.
head: environment

label: prop:kn
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kn}
For every \(n \ge 2\), 
\[
DRMS(K_n) = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{4}.
\]
where \(K_n\) denotes the complete graph on \(n\) vertices.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every singleton \(\{v\}\) is a minimal dominating set of \(K_n\): it is
dominating because \(v\) is adjacent to all other vertices, and it is minimal
because it contains no proper subset. Conversely, any dominating set \(S\) with
\(|S| \ge 2\) is not minimal, since \(S \setminus \{u\}\) still dominates
\(K_n\) for any \(u \in S\). Hence the minimal dominating sets of \(K_n\) are
exactly the singletons, so \(d_d(v) = 1\) for every \(v \in V(K_n)\).\\
Since \(d_d^2(u) + d_d^2(v) = 2\) for every edge \(uv\), and
\(m = \binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2\), we obtain
\[
DRMS(K_n) = \sum_{uv \in E(K_n)} \frac{1}{2} = \frac{m}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{4}. \qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: prop:star
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(c\) be the center and \(l_1, \ldots, l_{n-1}\) the leaves of \(S_n\).
We claim that the minimal dominating sets of \(S_n\) are exactly
\[
S_c := \{c\}, \qquad S_L := \{l_1, \ldots, l_{n-1}\}.
\]
\emph{Both are minimal dominating sets.} The singleton \(\{c\}\) dominates
\(S_n\) (every leaf is adjacent to \(c\)) and is minimal (it has no proper
subset). The set \(S_L\) dominates \(S_n\) (each leaf dominates itself, and
\(c\) is adjacent to every leaf in \(S_L\)); it is minimal because removing
any leaf \(l_i\) leaves \(l_i\) undominated (the leaves are pairwise
non-adjacent and \(c \notin S_L\)).\\
\emph{No other minimal dominating set exists.} Let \(S\) be a minimal
dominating set of \(S_n\). If \(c \in S\), then \(S = \{c\}\) by minimality
(since \(\{c\}\) already dominates \(S_n\)). If \(c \notin S\), then every
leaf \(l_i\) must belong to \(S\) (a leaf is adjacent only to \(c\), which is
not in \(S\)); hence \(S \supseteq S_L\), and minimality forces \(S = S_L\).\\
Consequently \(d_d(c) = 1\) (only \(S_c\) contains \(c\)) and
\(d_d(l_i) = 1\) (only \(S_L\) contains \(l_i\)), so \(d_d(v) = 1\) for every
\(v \in V(S_n)\). Since \(S_n\) has \(m = n-1\) edges and every edge
contributes \(1/(1^2 + 1^2) = 1/2\),
\[
DRMS(S_n) = \frac{m}{2} = \frac{n-1}{2}. \qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: prop:double-star
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:double-star}
For every \(p, q \ge 1\), 
\[
DRMS(S_{p,q}) = \frac{p+q+1}{8}.
\]
where \(S_{p,q}\) denotes the double-star graph formed by joining the centres
of two stars \(K_{1,p}\) and \(K_{1,q}\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(c_1, c_2\) be the two centers, \(l_1, \ldots, l_p\) the leaves adjacent
to \(c_1\), and \(l'_1, \ldots, l'_q\) the leaves adjacent to \(c_2\). We claim
that the minimal dominating sets of \(S_{p,q}\) are exactly
\[
S_1 = \{c_1, c_2\}, \quad
S_2 = \{c_1\} \cup \{l'_1, \ldots, l'_q\}, \quad
S_3 = \{c_2\} \cup \{l_1, \ldots, l_p\}, \quad
S_4 = \{l_1, \ldots, l_p, l'_1, \ldots, l'_q\}.
\]
Each of these dominates \(S_{p,q}\) and is minimal (removing any vertex
leaves either a leaf undominated or a center that is the only dominator of
its leaves).\\
Conversely, let \(S\) be a minimal dominating set. If \(c_1, c_2 \in S\),
then \(S = S_1\) by minimality. If \(c_1 \in S\) but \(c_2 \notin S\), every
leaf \(l'_j\) must belong to \(S\) (it is adjacent only to \(c_2\), which is
not in \(S\)), so \(S \supseteq \{c_1\} \cup \{l'_1, \ldots, l'_q\} = S_2\);
minimality forces \(S = S_2\). The case \(c_2 \in S\), \(c_1 \notin S\) is
symmetric and gives \(S = S_3\). Finally, if \(c_1, c_2 \notin S\), then every
leaf must belong to \(S\), so \(S = S_4\). Hence there are exactly four
minimal dominating sets.\\
Counting incidences, each vertex lies in exactly two of them:
\(c_1 \in S_1, S_2\); \(c_2 \in S_1, S_3\); each \(l_i \in S_3, S_4\); each
\(l'_j \in S_2, S_4\). Therefore \(d_d(v) = 2\) for every \(v \in V(S_{p,q})\).
Since \(S_{p,q}\) has \(m = p + q + 1\) edges and every edge contributes
\(1/(2^2 + 2^2) = 1/8\),
\[
DRMS(S_{p,q}) = \frac{m}{8} = \frac{p+q+1}{8}. \qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: prop:kmn
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kmn}
For every \(m, n \ge 2\),
\[
DRMS(K_{m,n}) = \frac{mn}{(m+1)^2 + (n+1)^2}.
\]
where \(K_{m,n}\) denotes the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes
\(m\) and \(n\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(V_1, V_2\) be the two parts of \(K_{m,n}\), with \(|V_1| = m\) and
\(|V_2| = n\). We first determine the minimal dominating sets of \(K_{m,n}\).
We claim they are exactly:
\[
V_1, \qquad V_2, \qquad \{v, w\} \text{ with } v \in V_1,\ w \in V_2.
\]
\emph{Each is a minimal dominating set.} The set \(V_1\) dominates \(K_{m,n}\)
(every vertex of \(V_2\) is adjacent to all of \(V_1\)) and is minimal
(removing any \(v \in V_1\) leaves \(v\) undominated, since \(v\) is adjacent
only to \(V_2\), which is disjoint from \(V_1\)). The same argument applies
to \(V_2\). For \(\{v, w\}\), domination holds because every vertex of \(V_1\)
is adjacent to \(w\) and every vertex of \(V_2\) is adjacent to \(v\).
Minimality holds because neither \(\{v\}\) nor \(\{w\}\) dominates: \(V_1
\setminus \{v\}\) is undominated by \(\{w\}\) (its vertices are adjacent only
to \(V_2\), and \(w \in V_2\) alone does not cover them), and symmetrically
for \(\{v\}\).\\
\emph{No other minimal dominating set exists.} Let \(S\) be a minimal
dominating set. If \(S \subseteq V_1\), then for every \(v \in V_1 \setminus S\)
to be dominated, some vertex of \(S\) must be adjacent to it; but no vertex
of \(V_1\) is adjacent to \(v\). Hence \(S = V_1\). Symmetrically for
\(S \subseteq V_2\). If \(S\) meets both \(V_1\) and \(V_2\), say \(v \in S
\cap V_1\) and \(w \in S \cap V_2\), then \(\{v, w\} \subseteq S\) already
dominates \(K_{m,n}\), so minimality forces \(S = \{v, w\}\).\\
\emph{Domination degrees.} A vertex \(v \in V_1\) lies in \(V_1\) and in the
\(n\) pairs \(\{v, w\}\) with \(w \in V_2\), hence \(d_d(v) = n + 1\).
Symmetrically, \(d_d(w) = m + 1\) for \(w \in V_2\).\\
\emph{DRMS.} Every edge \(vw\) with \(v \in V_1\), \(w \in V_2\) contributes
\[
\frac{1}{d_d^2(v) + d_d^2(w)} = \frac{1}{(n+1)^2 + (m+1)^2},
\]
and there are \(mn\) such edges. Hence
\[
DRMS(K_{m,n}) = \frac{mn}{(m+1)^2 + (n+1)^2}. \qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: def:kpartite
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:kpartite}
For \(k \ge 2\) and \(r_1, \ldots, r_k \ge 2\), the \emph{complete
\(k\)-partite graph} \(K_{r_1, \dots, r_k}\) has vertex set partitioned into
\(k\) parts \(V_1, \ldots, V_k\) of sizes \(r_1, \ldots, r_k\), with two
vertices adjacent if and only if they lie in different parts. We write
\(N = \sum_{i=1}^k r_i\).
head: environment

label: lem:kpartite-mds
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:kpartite-mds}
Let \(G = K_{r_1, \dots, r_k}\) with \(k \ge 2\) and all \(r_i \ge 2\). The
minimal dominating sets of \(G\) are exactly the parts \(V_l\) and the pairs
\(\{u, w\}\) with \(u, w\) in different parts.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(V_1, \ldots, V_k\) be the parts.\\
\emph{Domination.} If \(u \in V_i\), \(w \in V_j\), \(i \neq j\), then
\(\{u, w\}\) dominates \(G\): vertices of \(V_i\) are adjacent to \(w\),
vertices of \(V_j\) to \(u\), and all other vertices to both. Each \(V_l\)
dominates \(G\), since every vertex outside \(V_l\) is adjacent to all of
\(V_l\).\\
\emph{Minimality.} Removing \(u \in V_l\) from \(V_l\) leaves \(u\)
undominated. For \(\{u, w\}\) as above, \(\{w\}\) does not dominate the
vertices of \(V_j \setminus \{w\}\) (nonempty because \(r_j \geq 2\)), and
\(\{u\}\) does not dominate \(V_i \setminus \{u\}\) (because \(r_i \geq 2\)).\\
\emph{Completeness.} Let \(S\) be a minimal dominating set. If \(S\) meets two
different parts, it contains a dominating pair, so \(S\) equals that pair by
minimality. Otherwise \(S \subseteq V_l\) for some \(l\); a vertex of \(V_l\)
is dominated by \(S\) only if it lies in \(S\) (it is not adjacent to anything
in \(V_l\)), hence \(S \supseteq V_l\) and \(S = V_l\).
head: environment

label: lem:kpartite-dd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:kpartite-dd}
Under the notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:kpartite-mds}, for every vertex \(v\) in
the \(l\)-th part,
\[
d_d(v) = N - r_l + 1,
\]
where \(N = \sum_i r_i\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:kpartite-mds}, the minimal dominating sets of \(G\) are the
parts \(V_1, \ldots, V_k\) and the pairs \(\{u, w\}\) with \(u, w\) in
different parts.\\
A vertex \(v \in V_l\) lies in the set \(V_l\) and in the \(N - r_l\) pairs
\(\{v, w\}\) with \(w \notin V_l\). No other minimal dominating set contains
\(v\). Hence \(d_d(v) = 1 + (N - r_l) = N - r_l + 1\).
head: environment

label: thm:kpartite
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:kpartite}
Let \(G = K_{r_1, \dots, r_k}\) with \(k \ge 2\) and all \(r_i \ge 2\), and
let \(N = \sum_i r_i\). Then
\[
DRMS(G) = \sum_{1 \le l < j \le k} \frac{r_l r_j}{(N - r_l + 1)^2 + (N - r_j + 1)^2}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $V_1,\dots,V_k$ be the parts. We claim that the minimal dominating sets
are exactly the parts $V_l$ and the pairs $\{u,w\}$ with $u,w$ in different
parts.\\
\emph{Domination.} If $u\in V_i$, $w\in V_j$, $i\ne j$, then $\{u,w\}$
dominates $G$: vertices of $V_i$ are adjacent to $w$, vertices of $V_j$ to
$u$, and all other vertices to both. Each $V_l$ dominates $G$, since every
vertex outside $V_l$ is adjacent to all of $V_l$.\\
\emph{Minimality.} Removing $u\in V_l$ from $V_l$ leaves $u$ undominated.
For $\{u,w\}$ as above, $\{w\}$ does not dominate the vertices of $V_j\setminus\{w\}$
(nonempty because $r_j\ge2$), and $\{u\}$ does not dominate
$V_i\setminus\{u\}$ (because $r_i\ge2$).\\
\emph{Completeness.} Let $S$ be a minimal dominating set. If $S$ meets two
different parts, it contains a dominating pair, so $S$ equals that pair by
minimality. Otherwise $S\subseteq V_l$ for some $l$; a vertex of $V_l$ is
dominated by $S$ only if it lies in $S$ (it is not adjacent to anything in
$V_l$), hence $S\supseteq V_l$ and $S=V_l$.\\
\emph{Counting.} A vertex $v\in V_l$ lies in the set $V_l$ and in the $N-r_l$
pairs $\{v,w\}$ with $w\notin V_l$, so $d_d(v)=N-r_l+1$. There are $r_lr_j$
edges between $V_l$ and $V_j$, each contributing
$1/\bigl((N-r_l+1)^2+(N-r_j+1)^2\bigr)$.

label: def:wheel
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:wheel}
For \(n \ge 4\), the \emph{wheel graph} \(W_n\) consists of a cycle
\(C_{n-1}\) with vertices \(v_1, \dots, v_{n-1}\) together with a central
vertex \(v_0\) adjacent to every vertex of the cycle.
head: environment

label: def:tk
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:tk}
For $k\ge 3$, fix a vertex $x$ of the cycle $C_k$ and define
\[
t_k = \mathrm{card}\{S \subseteq V(C_k) : S \text{ is a minimal dominating set of } C_k,\ x \in S\}.
\]
Since $C_k$ is vertex-transitive, $t_k$ does not depend on the choice of $x$.
head: environment

label: lem:wheel
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:nbr
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S\subseteq V(C_{n-1})$, so $v_0\notin S$. For every cycle vertex $v_i$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nbr}
  N_{W_n}[v_i]\cap S \;=\; N_{C_{n-1}}[v_i]\cap S,
\end{equation}
because the only additional neighbour of $v_i$ in $W_n$ is $v_0\notin S$.\\
Domination.
By \eqref{eq:nbr}, a cycle vertex is dominated by $S$ in $W_n$ if and only if it is dominated by $S$ in $C_{n-1}$. The centre $v_0$ is adjacent to every vertex of $C_{n-1}$, so it is dominated by every nonempty $S\subseteq V(C_{n-1})$. Every dominating set of $C_{n-1}$ is nonempty. Hence
\[
  S \text{ dominates } W_n \text{ if and only if } S \text{ dominates } C_{n-1}.
\]
\medskip
Minimality.
Assume that $S$ dominates both graphs. By Lemma~\ref{lem:private} (a dominating set is minimal if and only if every vertex of it has a private neighbour), it suffices to compare the private neighbours of each $u\in S$ in the two graphs. Let $w\in V(W_n)$ satisfy $N_{W_n}[w]\cap S=\{u\}$.\\
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $w\in V(C_{n-1})$, then by \eqref{eq:nbr} we get $N_{C_{n-1}}[w]\cap S=\{u\}$. Thus $w$ is also a private neighbour of $u$ in $C_{n-1}$. Conversely, every private neighbour of $u$ in $C_{n-1}$ is a private neighbour of $u$ in $W_n$, again by \eqref{eq:nbr}.
  \item If $w=v_0$, then $N_{W_n}[v_0]\cap S=S$, so $S=\{u\}$. A one-element dominating set is always minimal, since $\emptyset$ is not dominating. Hence $S$ is minimal in $W_n$. Moreover, $S=\{u\}$ dominates $C_{n-1}$ and is therefore minimal there as well. (This case occurs only for $n=4$, i.e.\ $W_4=K_4$.)
\end{itemize}
Consequently, if $|S|\ge 2$, then $v_0$ is never a private neighbour, and $u\in S$ has a private neighbour in $W_n$ if and only if it has one in $C_{n-1}$. If $|S|=1$, then $S$ is minimal in both graphs. In all cases,
\[
  S \text{ is minimal in } W_n \text{ if and only if } S \text{ is minimal in } C_{n-1}.
\]
Together with the domination equivalence, this proves the lemma.
head: environment

label: thm:wheel-dd
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:wheel-dd}
Let \(W_n\) be the wheel graph with centre \(v_0\) and cycle vertices
\(v_1, \ldots, v_{n-1}\). For \(n \ge 4\),
\[
d_d(v_0) = 1, \qquad d_d(v_i) = t_{n-1} \quad (1 \le i \le n-1).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The set $\{v_0\}$ is the only minimal dominating set of $W_n$ containing
$v_0$, so $d_d(v_0)=1$. Let $v_i$ be a cycle vertex with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and let $S$ be a minimal dominating set of $W_n$ containing $v_i$. If
$v_0\in S$, then by minimality of $S$ we must have $S=\{v_0\}$, which
contradicts $v_i\in S$. Hence $v_0\notin S$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:wheel}
$S$ is a minimal dominating set of $C_{n-1}$ containing $v_i$. Conversely,
every minimal dominating set of $C_{n-1}$ containing $v_i$ is a minimal
dominating set of $W_n$ containing $v_i$. Therefore the number of such sets
is exactly $t_{n-1}$.
head: environment

label: thm:wheel
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The wheel $W_n$ has $2(n-1)$ edges: $n-1$ spokes joining $v_0$ to the cycle
vertices, and $n-1$ edges of the cycle $C_{n-1}$. Using the domination
degrees from Theorem~\ref{thm:wheel-dd},
\[
DRMS(W_n)
=(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{1+t_{n-1}^2}
+(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{2t_{n-1}^2}.
\]
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
For $W_6$, we have $t_5=2$, hence $d_d(v_0)=1$ and $d_d(v_i)=2$ for
$1\le i\le 5$, and
\[
DRMS(W_6)=5\left(\frac15+\frac18\right)=\frac{13}{8}=1.625.
\]
head: environment

label: def:book
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:book}
For \(r \ge 2\), the \emph{book graph} \(B_r\) consists of two adjacent
\emph{hub} vertices \(a, b\), together with \(2r\) \emph{page} vertices
\(p_1, \ldots, p_r\) and \(p'_1, \ldots, p'_r\), where \(p_i\) is adjacent
to \(a\), \(p'_i\) is adjacent to \(b\), and \(p_i\) is adjacent to \(p'_i\)
for each \(i\). The graph has \(2(r+1)\) vertices and \(3r+1\) edges.
head: environment

label: lem:book-mds
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:book-mds}
\(B_r\) has exactly \(2^r + 3\) minimal dominating sets, namely
\[
\{a,b\}; \quad \{a,p_1,\dots,p_r\}; \quad \{a,p_1',\dots,p_r'\};
\]
\[
\{b,p_1,\dots,p_r\}; \quad \{b,p_1',\dots,p_r'\};
\]
and the \(2^r - 2\) sets
\[
S_J = \{p_i : i \in J\} \cup \{p_i' : i \notin J\},
\qquad \varnothing \neq J \subsetneq [r].
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note \(N[a] = \{a, b, p_1, \dots, p_r\}\), \(N[b] = \{b, a, p_1', \dots, p_r'\}\),
\(N[p_i] = \{p_i, a, p_i'\}\), \(N[p_i'] = \{p_i', b, p_i\}\). Let \(S\) be
minimal dominating.

\emph{Case \(a, b \in S\).} \(\{a,b\}\) already dominates \(G\), so
\(S = \{a,b\}\); it is minimal since \(\{a\}\) misses \(p_i'\) and \(\{b\}\)
misses \(p_i\).

\emph{Case \(a \in S\), \(b \notin S\).} Every \(p_i'\) must be dominated, so
\(S \cap \{p_i, p_i'\} \neq \varnothing\) for all \(i\). A private neighbour of
\(a\) lies in \(N[a]\): the vertex \(a\) itself works if and only if \(S\) contains no
\(p_i\); the vertex \(b\) works if and only if \(S\) contains no \(p_i'\); a vertex
\(p_i\) never works since \(S \cap \{p_i, p_i'\} \neq \varnothing\) and
\(\{p_i, p_i'\} \subseteq N[p_i]\) with \(a \in S\). Hence either no
\(p_i \in S\), forcing \(S \supseteq \{a, p_1', \dots, p_r'\}\), or no
\(p_i' \in S\), forcing \(S \supseteq \{a, p_1, \dots, p_r\}\). These sets are
dominating, so \(S\) equals one of them, and both are minimal: in
\(\{a, p_1', \dots, p_r'\}\) the vertex \(a\) is its own private neighbour and
each \(p_i'\) is its own private neighbour; in \(\{a, p_1, \dots, p_r\}\) the
vertex \(a\) has the private neighbour \(b\) and \(p_i\) has the private
neighbour \(p_i'\).

\emph{Case \(b \in S\), \(a \notin S\).} Symmetric: two sets.

\emph{Case \(a, b \notin S\).} To dominate \(p_i\) and \(p_i'\) we need
\(S \cap \{p_i, p_i'\} \neq \varnothing\) for every \(i\). Suppose
\(p_i, p_i' \in S\) for some \(i\). A private neighbour of \(p_i\) in
\(N[p_i] = \{p_i, a, p_i'\}\) can only be \(a\) (the others are dominated by
\(p_i'\)), which requires \(p_i\) to be the only \(p\) in \(S\); likewise
\(p_i'\) needs \(b\), i.e.\ \(p_i'\) is the only \(p'\) in \(S\). Then for
\(j \neq i\) (such \(j\) exists as \(r \geq 2\)) neither \(p_j\) nor
\(p_j'\) lies in \(S\), a contradiction. So exactly one of \(p_i, p_i'\) lies
in \(S\) for each \(i\): \(S = S_J\). Domination of \(a\) and \(b\) requires
\(J \neq \varnothing\) and \(J \neq [r]\). Conversely each such \(S_J\) is
dominating and minimal (\(p_i\) has the private neighbour \(p_i'\) and vice
versa).
head: environment

label: lem:book-dd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:book-dd}
For every \(r \geq 2\),
\[
d_d(a) = d_d(b) = 3, \qquad d_d(p_i) = d_d(p_i') = 2^{r-1} + 1 =: q.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:book-mds}, \(a\) lies in \(\{a,b\}\) and in the two sets of
the second case: \(d_d(a) = 3\); same for \(b\). A vertex \(p_i\) lies in one
set of the second case, one of the third, and in \(S_J\) for \(i \in J \neq [r]\),
i.e.\ \(2^{r-1} - 1\) sets: \(d_d(p_i) = 2^{r-1} + 1\). By symmetry,
\(d_d(p_i') = 2^{r-1} + 1\).
head: environment

label: thm:book
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:book}
For every \(r \geq 2\),
\[
DRMS(B_r) = \frac{1}{18} + \frac{2r}{9 + q^2} + \frac{r}{2q^2},
\qquad q = 2^{r-1} + 1.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:book-dd}, the edge classes are \(ab\) (weight \(1/18\)),
\(2r\) hub--page edges (weight \(1/(9 + q^2)\)) and \(r\) edges
\(p_i p_i'\) (weight \(1/(2q^2)\)). Summing over all edges,
\[
DRMS(B_r) = \frac{1}{18} + \frac{2r}{9 + q^2} + \frac{r}{2q^2}.
\]
head: environment

label: def:butterfly
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:butterfly}
For \(r, s \ge 1\), the \emph{butterfly graph} \(B_{r,s}\) is formed by
taking a central vertex \(c\), attaching to it \(r\) triangles
\(c x_i y_i c\) that are pairwise disjoint except for \(c\), and attaching
to it \(s\) pendant vertices \(z_1, \ldots, z_s\). The graph has
\(2r + s + 1\) vertices and \(3r + s\) edges.
head: environment

label: thm:butterfly
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:butterfly}
The minimal dominating sets of $B_{r,s}$ are $\{c\}$ and the $2^r$ sets
consisting of $\{z_1,\dots,z_s\}$ together with exactly one of $x_i,y_i$ for
each $i$. Therefore $d_d(c)=1$, $d_d(x_i)=d_d(y_i)=2^{r-1}$, $d_d(z_j)=2^r$ and
\[
DRMS(B_{r,s})=\frac{s}{1+4^{r}}+\frac{2r}{1+4^{r-1}}+\frac{r}{2\cdot4^{r-1}}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $c\in S$ then $S=\{c\}$ because $\{c\}$ dominates $G$ (and it is minimal,
since $z_1$ is not dominated without $c$ or $z_1$). Let $c\notin S$. Since
$N[z_j]=\{z_j,c\}$, all $z_j\in S$ (this also dominates $c$, as $s\ge1$). For
each triangle, $S\cap\{x_i,y_i\}\ne\varnothing$. If both $x_i,y_i\in S$, then
$x_i$ has no private neighbour (its closed neighbourhood $\{x_i,y_i,c\}$ is
dominated also by $y_i$ or $z_1$), contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:private}. So
exactly one is chosen. Conversely, such a set is dominating, $z_j$ is its own
private neighbour and $x_i$ (resp.\ $y_i$) has the private neighbour $y_i$
(resp.\ $x_i$). Counting: $c$ lies in one set; each $z_j$ in all $2^r$ sets of
the second type; each $x_i$ in half of them. The edge classes are $s$ edges
$cz_j$ with $x_e=1+4^r$, $2r$ edges $cx_i,cy_i$ with $x_e=1+4^{r-1}$, and $r$
edges $x_iy_i$ with $x_e=2\cdot4^{r-1}$.
head: environment

label: def:corona
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:corona}
Let \(G\) be a graph of order \(n_1\) and size \(m_1\), and let \(F\) be any
graph. The \emph{corona} \(G \circ F\) is obtained by taking, for each vertex
\(v \in V(G)\), one copy \(F^v\) of \(F\), with the copies being pairwise
disjoint, and joining \(v\) to every vertex of \(F^v\). The resulting graph has
\[
|V(G \circ F)| = n_1 (1 + |V(F)|), \qquad
|E(G \circ F)| = m_1 + n_1 \cdot |E(F)| + n_1 \cdot |V(F)|.
\]
head: environment

label: thm:corona
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:corona}
Let $G$ be connected, $n_2\ge1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G\circ K_{n_2}$ has exactly $(n_2+1)^{n_1}$ minimal dominating sets and
is $k$-domination-regular with $k=(n_2+1)^{n_1-1}$. It has
$m_1+n_1n_2(n_2+1)/2$ edges, so
\[
DRMS(G\circ K_{n_2})=
\frac{m_1+n_1n_2(n_2+1)/2}{2\,(n_2+1)^{2(n_1-1)}}.
\]
\item $G\circ\overline{K_{n_2}}$ has exactly $2^{n_1}$ minimal dominating sets
and is $2^{n_1-1}$-domination-regular, with $m_1+n_1n_2$ edges:
\[
DRMS(G\circ\overline{K_{n_2}})=\frac{m_1+n_1n_2}{2^{\,2n_1-1}}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) For $v\in V(G)$ let $B_v=\{v\}\cup V(F^v)$; it is a clique with
$n_2+1\ge2$ vertices, and the sets $B_v$ partition $V(H)$, $H=G\circ K_{n_2}$.
Let $S$ be minimal dominating. A vertex $t\in V(F^v)$ has $N[t]=B_v$, so
$S\cap B_v\ne\varnothing$. If $|S\cap B_v|\ge2$, then $S\cap B_v$ contains a
non-centre $t\in F^v$, and $t$ has no private neighbour ($N[t]=B_v$ contains
another element of $S$) -- contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:private}. Hence
$|S\cap B_v|=1$ for all $v$. Conversely, any choice of one vertex per block is
dominating, and it is minimal: a chosen $t\in F^v$ is its own private
neighbour, while a chosen $v$ has any vertex of $F^v$ as a private neighbour
($N[t]=B_v$ meets $S$ only in $v$). Thus there are $(n_2+1)^{n_1}$ minimal
dominating sets, and a vertex of $B_v$ lies in those that choose it:
$(n_2+1)^{n_1-1}$ sets. The edge count is $m_1+n_1n_2+n_1\binom{n_2}{2}$.

(2) Let $P_v$ be the $n_2$ pendant vertices at $v$. Since $N[p]=\{p,v\}$ for
$p\in P_v$, we have $S\cap(\{v\}\cup P_v)\ne\varnothing$. If $v\in S$ and some
$p\in S$, then $p$ has no private neighbour; so $v\in S\Rightarrow
S\cap P_v=\varnothing$, and $v\notin S\Rightarrow P_v\subseteq S$. Thus $S$ is
determined by $A=S\cap V(G)$, namely $S_A=A\cup\bigcup_{v\notin A}P_v$, and
every $A\subseteq V(G)$ gives a dominating set. It is minimal: $p\in P_v$ with
$v\notin A$ is its own private neighbour, and $v\in A$ has any $p\in P_v$ as a
private neighbour. Hence there are $2^{n_1}$ minimal dominating sets and each
vertex lies in $2^{n_1-1}$ of them.
head: environment
